title: The examen
hookLine: Ignatius of Loyola's nightly review looks for gratitude before faults (Spiritual Exercises 43)

cards: At the siege of Pamplona, a Spanish soldier named Iñigo was hit by a cannonball that shattered his leg. Bored in bed through the long months of recovery, he asked for novels about knights. The house didn't have any.
It had a life of Christ and a book of saints. He read them, and something in him turned. He became Ignatius of Loyola, and later founded the Jesuits, a Catholic religious order.
He also wrote a little handbook, the Spiritual Exercises, and in it is an evening review that people still pray. Its first step comes before any talk of faults.

teach.h: EXAMEN: THE NEEDLE ON THE SCALES.
teach.b: Examen is Latin for an examination. It also meant the needle on a set of scales, the little pointer that shows which way things are tipping: a good picture for a daily look at which way your life is leaning.
In the Spiritual Exercises, section 43, Ignatius lays out five points.
The first, in paraphrase: give thanks to God for the good things you have received.

Only after that: ask for light to see your faults, go over the day hour by hour, ask forgiveness, and resolve to do better tomorrow. Put that beside this week's reviews. Sextius began with what you cured.
The Golden Verses began with where you slipped. Ignatius begins with thanks. Before you look for what went wrong, you look for what was given.
Why start there? Catholics and other Christians who pray the examen would say it's because the whole review happens in the presence of a loving God, and gratitude puts you where you can see that.
You don't have to share that belief to notice what the order does. Start with faults, and the mind tends to stay in the courtroom.
Start with what was good today, the coffee, the kind text, the moment the light came through the window, and you meet your faults from somewhere steadier.
Today the examen is prayed by Jesuits, by other Catholics, and by some Protestants too, often in a shorter modern form. For those who pray it, it is a prayer, not a technique.

how: Jesuits pray the examen, usually daily, and other Catholics and some Protestants use it too, often in a short form: give thanks, ask for light, review the day, ask forgiveness, and look ahead to tomorrow.

games.q: you're Ignatius, recovering in bed with a shattered leg. you asked for novels about knights, but the house has none. what do you do?
o: demand someone go and buy some.
read the lives of Christ and the saints.
games.why: he read them, and something in him turned. the soldier became Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits.

practice: Go back over the last day, and before anything else, find its best moment, even a tiny one, a laugh, a good meal, a text from someone, and stay with it for a few breaths, glad.
If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's way. Only then, if something went wrong, look at it gently, from there.

wordCard.voice: Examen. Latin for an examination, and the needle on a scale; Ignatius's nightly review, which begins with thanks. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: an examination, a weighing; also the needle or tongue of a balance, the pointer that shows which way it tips.

carryVoice: Your line: gratitude first. The faults look different from there. Day one hundred eight, done.
